content_html:
A daily worship tracker is a simple plan that spreads your acts of worship across the day, so you know what to do after each prayer and can see what you actually did, instead of relying on bursts of motivation. This guide gives you a practical schedule built around the five prayer times, a printable weekly tracker, and proven tips for turning worship into a lasting habit.

Every item is based on authentic Sunnah, and the plan is designed to be realistic for people who work, study or care for young children, because the goal is consistency, not short-lived intensity. Quran translations are from Sahih International; hadith translations are of the meaning.

How do I build a daily worship schedule?

  1. Pray the five daily prayers on time; they are the foundation.
  2. Add the 12 regular Sunnah rak'ahs (rawatib).
  3. Say the morning adhkar after Fajr and the evening adhkar after Asr.
  4. Set a fixed daily Quran portion, even two pages.
  5. Do the tasbih after each prayer and make du'a.
  6. End the day with Witr and the bedtime adhkar.
  7. Tick off what you did each night and review weekly.

These seven steps are the skeleton. Below, we explain each one, tie it to a time and its evidence, and then put everything into one table you can print or copy.

Why does a Muslim need a worship plan?

﴿وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الْجِنَّ وَالْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ﴾

"And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me." [Surah adh-Dhariyat 51:56, Sahih International]

Worship is not a few scattered days of zeal but a lifelong path: "And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty" [Surah al-Hijr 15:99]. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said:

"Do good deeds properly, sincerely and moderately, and know that your deeds alone will not admit you to Paradise, and that the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most consistent, even if small." (Sahih al-Bukhari 6464)

A tracker gives you three things:

  • Clarity: you decide in advance what happens after Fajr, after Asr and before sleep, so no time is lost wondering.
  • Self-accounting: "O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow" [Surah al-Hashr 59:18, Sahih International]. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have said, "Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account," a saying at-Tirmidhi mentions in his Sunan.
  • Gradual growth: when you can see your record week after week, you can add a new act of worship knowing the earlier ones are stable.

Which acts of worship come first?

The obligations come first. In a hadith qudsi Allah says: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him, and My servant keeps drawing near to Me with voluntary deeds until I love him" (Sahih al-Bukhari 6502).

The five prayers on time

"Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times" [Surah an-Nisa 4:103, Sahih International]. Prayer is also the first deed a servant will be judged on, as in the hadith reported by at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i. So let each prayer box in your tracker mean "prayed on time", not just "prayed". For men who can attend the mosque, praying in congregation carries far greater reward.

The regular Sunnah prayers (rawatib)

"There is no Muslim servant who prays for Allah every day twelve rak'ahs of voluntary prayer, other than the obligatory, except that Allah builds for him a house in Paradise." (Sahih Muslim 728)

At-Tirmidhi's narration details them: four before Dhuhr and two after, two after Maghrib, two after Isha, and two before Fajr. The greatest is the Sunnah of Fajr: "The two rak'ahs of Fajr are better than this world and everything in it" (Sahih Muslim 725).

Adhkar, Quran and du'a

Next come the morning and evening adhkar, which we list with counts and sources in morning and evening adhkar: virtues and timing. Then a daily Quran portion: "Recite the Quran, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions" (Sahih Muslim 804). Then du'a, for "Du'a is worship" (Abu Dawud; at-Tirmidhi).

A daily worship schedule built around prayer times

The most reliable way to organise the day is to attach each act of worship to a prayer. Prayer times are fixed anchors, so each prayer becomes the "alarm" for what follows it. In total, this plan takes roughly one to one and a half hours spread across the day:

TimeWorshipApprox. durationEvidence or virtue
Before FajrTwo Sunnah rak'ahs of Fajr; du'a before dawn if possible5–10 min"Better than this world and everything in it" (Muslim 725)
After FajrPost-prayer dhikr, morning adhkar, Quran portion20–30 min"Exalt your Lord before the rising of the sun" [Qaf 50:39]
Mid-morning (Duha)Two rak'ahs of Duha, from when the sun has risen until shortly before Dhuhr5 minThe Prophet's advice to Abu Hurayrah (al-Bukhari 1981; Muslim 721)
DhuhrFour rak'ahs before, two after, post-prayer dhikr10–15 minThe rawatib (Muslim 728)
AsrPost-prayer dhikr, then evening adhkar10–15 min"...and before its setting" [Qaf 50:39]
MaghribTwo rak'ahs after; du'a and family time10 minThe rawatib
IshaTwo rak'ahs after, then Witr if you may not wake at night10–15 min"Make Witr your last prayer at night" (al-Bukhari and Muslim)
Before sleepBedtime adhkar; a quick self-review and tick the tracker5–10 min"Let every soul look to what it has put forth" [al-Hashr 59:18]

After every obligatory prayer, the tasbih taught by the Prophet ﷺ is recommended:

"Whoever glorifies Allah (SubhanAllah) after every prayer thirty-three times, praises Allah (Alhamdulillah) thirty-three times and magnifies Allah (Allahu akbar) thirty-three times, that is ninety-nine, and completes the hundred with La ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-hamd, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir, his sins will be forgiven even if they are like the foam of the sea." (Sahih Muslim 597)

Light deeds to fill idle moments

  • Istighfar: "By Allah, I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times a day" (Sahih al-Bukhari 6307).
  • Salawat on the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever sends one blessing upon me, Allah sends ten upon him" (Sahih Muslim 408).
  • Charity, even a little: "Charity does not decrease wealth" (Sahih Muslim 2588).
  • Listening to the Quran on your commute or during chores.

Printable weekly worship tracker

Copy or print this table and keep it somewhere you see daily. Put a tick (✓) in the box when you complete an item. The first rows are the essentials; the last row is optional, depending on your capacity:

WorshipMonTueWedThuFriSatSun
Fajr on time
Dhuhr on time
Asr on time
Maghrib on time
Isha on time
Rawatib (12 rak'ahs)
Morning adhkar
Evening adhkar
Quran portion
Du'a
Witr
Optional: Duha / charity / Monday-Thursday fast

On fasting Mondays and Thursdays, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Deeds are presented on Monday and Thursday, and I love for my deeds to be presented while I am fasting" (at-Tirmidhi). If you add it, start with one day a week.

Example: a day for someone who starts work at 8 a.m.

Wake ten minutes before Fajr, pray the Sunnah and make du'a. Pray Fajr, then the post-prayer dhikr and morning adhkar, then two pages of Quran before getting ready. Listen to a surah or make istighfar on the commute. Pray Dhuhr and its Sunnah during the lunch break, and Asr on the way home, followed by the evening adhkar. After Maghrib, spend time with family; after Isha, pray its Sunnah and Witr, say the bedtime adhkar and tick the tracker. The whole day adds about an hour and a quarter of worship, yet covers the obligations, the rawatib, the adhkar and a Quran portion.

How do I make worship a habit that lasts?

Many people start with enthusiasm and stop after a few days. The cause is usually poor planning, not weak faith. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The religion is easy, and no one makes the religion too hard for himself except that it overcomes him. So be moderate, do your best, and rejoice" (Sahih al-Bukhari 39). Practical tips:

  1. Start very small. One page of Quran a day beats a full juz' you abandon after a week. The family of the Prophet ﷺ, when they began a deed, kept it up, as Muslim reports.
  2. Stack it onto a fixed habit. "After I finish the Fajr prayer, I say the morning adhkar." A specific rule like this is far stronger than a vague intention to "remember Allah more".
  3. Add one new item every two weeks. Do not fill the whole tracker on day one. Secure the prayers on time, then add the rawatib, then the adhkar, then the Quran portion.
  4. Shape your environment. Keep a mushaf in sight, set an alarm ten minutes before Fajr, and keep your phone away from the bed if it delays your sleep.
  5. Never miss twice. If you miss a day, do not let it become two. Seeing an unbroken streak motivates you, but a broken streak is not the end of the road.
  6. Find good company. Agree on a shared routine with a friend or your family and gently check in on each other.
  7. Review weekly. Each Friday, look at your tracker: what held, what slipped, and why? Adjust the plan instead of blaming yourself.

The My Deeds section of the Rafiq Al-Taa app was built for exactly this: a daily checklist of the five prayers, adhkar, Quran reading and du'a that ticks itself as you use the app, with a streak counter and a 30-day record. Your data stays on your phone. Learn more in the best Islamic app without ads.

What if I fall behind on my daily routine?

Everyone slips; what matters is returning quickly without harsh self-blame. Islam allows making up missed devotions: "Whoever sleeps and misses his portion, or part of it, and recites it between the Fajr prayer and the Dhuhr prayer, it is recorded for him as though he had recited it at night" (Sahih Muslim 747). And 'A'ishah reported that when the Prophet ﷺ missed his night prayer because of pain or other reasons, he prayed twelve rak'ahs during the day (Sahih Muslim 746). A missed obligatory prayer due to sleep or forgetfulness must be made up as soon as you remember, while making up voluntary devotions is recommended.

Does tracking worship conflict with sincerity?

No, as long as tracking is a tool for self-accounting and not for showing off. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Actions are only by intentions" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1; Sahih Muslim 1907). Keep your tracker private between you and your Lord; do not post your achievements, and do not make the numbers a goal in themselves. A sign of a sound intention is that the tracker makes you more humble and focused, not more pleased with yourself. That is why we prefer tools that keep your data on your own device, with no accounts or public sharing.

How do I adapt the plan to my situation?

Working professionals and students

Use the fixed points: morning adhkar on the commute, Dhuhr and its Sunnah during a break, and your Quran portion after Fajr before the day starts. In busy weeks, protect the essentials only: prayers on time and the adhkar.

Mothers of young children

You do not need to compete with people who have free time. Let dhikr accompany your daily tasks, and say the adhkar aloud so your children learn them with you. To involve them in prayer, see how to teach your child to pray.

Women during menstruation

Prayer is lifted during menstruation and postnatal bleeding and is not made up, by scholarly consensus. Other doors remain open: dhikr, istighfar, du'a, charity and listening to the Quran. Swap the prayer rows for these during those days so the habit is not broken.

Ramadan and special seasons

Increase in blessed seasons such as Ramadan and the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah: night prayer, a larger Quran portion and daily charity. But make sure you leave each season with one lasting addition.

Common mistakes and a final word

  • An overloaded "perfect" plan: plan for your worst days, not your best.
  • Voluntary before obligatory: there is little sense in guarding Duha while delaying Fajr past its time.
  • Numbers over khushu': two focused rak'ahs are better than many rushed ones just to fill a box.
  • Forgetting people's rights: honouring parents, keeping family ties and visiting the sick are great acts of worship; add a weekly row for them.
  • Giving up after one bad day: come back tomorrow; Allah loves those who repent.

A daily worship tracker is not a long list that wears you out. It is a realistic plan that starts with the five prayers on time, gradually adds the rawatib, adhkar, Quran and du'a, and ends each day with a short review. Print the weekly table or use a tool that tracks for you, and review every Friday. The rulings here summarise well-known scholarly positions; for personal circumstances, please consult trusted scholars in your community.

faq.q: What should a daily worship tracker include?
faq.a: Start with the five prayers on time, since they are the first obligation and the first deed judged. Then add the 12 rawatib rak'ahs, the morning and evening adhkar, a fixed Quran portion, du'a and Witr. Once these are steady, add Duha, charity and fasting on Mondays and Thursdays gradually.

faq.q: How much time does a daily worship plan take?
faq.a: The core plan takes about one to one and a half hours spread over the whole day, mostly a few minutes after each prayer. Consistency matters more than length: the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most consistent even if small, as in Sahih al-Bukhari. You can start with fifteen minutes and build up.

faq.q: What should I do if I miss my daily Quran portion?
faq.a: Make it up when you can. Sahih Muslim reports that whoever sleeps and misses his portion, then recites it between Fajr and Dhuhr, it is recorded as though he recited it at night. If you keep missing it, shrink the portion rather than dropping it, and never let one missed day become two.

faq.q: Is tracking my worship a form of showing off?
faq.a: No, if the tracker stays private between you and Allah and you use it for self-accounting, since actions are judged by intentions. Showing off is a concern when you publish your achievements for praise or treat the numbers as something to boast about. Keep it hidden, renew your intention and prefer a private tool.

faq.q: How can a woman keep her worship routine during her period?
faq.a: Prayer is lifted during menstruation and is not made up, by consensus. She can continue dhikr, istighfar, du'a, charity and listening to the Quran. It helps to replace the prayer rows in her tracker with these acts during those days, so the habit continues and returning to the full routine afterwards is easy.
